items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1959-10-26
items.q: In fact, I never knew Joe Oliver.

ctx.x: Did you ever see Jelly Roll Martin?

No, I never knew him. I never met him. In fact, I never knew Joe Oliver. I never met Pompous Celestine to La New Orleans Jazz Club down here, and Miss Menville introduced me to him. And she asked him, was this one of the men who used to sit down and listen to you? He said, no, ma'am. I never seen this man in my life before. I had already told her I never met him, but she didn't believe it, but she tried to put me on the spot. But that Negro had more honesty and truthfulness in his body than Miss Menville has in…
Was Celestine playing when you were a young man?

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-02
items.q: If this man heard them, Joe Oliver heard them.

ctx.x: I have a record of Virginia Blues by the Louisiana Five in which they play the third strain of Skeleton Jangle as a part of the tune. It's signed, uh, Sincerely Yours, Don Fowler. Is there anything else you want to read?

You know, that's all. Not only the Louisiana Five, but everybody. It was a field lead from the all steel music and different things out the original Dixieland jazz band. Now they say these Negroes didn't hear these records. Joe heard them. If this man heard them, Joe Oliver heard them. Because Joe, in his thing, that's what he bases his rhythm on. Because he didn't know no better. He was just a Negro that didn't know no better. Like these even white crumbs who's supposed to be historians around New Orleans. They…

The letter here from... Let me see. I'll give you the full letterhead. It's a letter from Marshall W. Stearns. Yale Hot Club, 6th Linwood Place, New Haven, Connecticut. M. W. Stearns, President. Charter Unit of the UHCA. January the 11th, 1937, Mr. D.J. La Rocca, Earl Theater, Washington, D.C. Dear Nick, I have all your records from Liberty Stable Blues to the recent disc. I like the earlier ones better. Between you and me, our last argument should furnish you with plenty of publicity. I do think, however, that…

We used to have swing sessions every morning around 3 o'clock after the boys got through with their work and each man would do his bit. Quote, the first hot band to leave from the South and introduce swing music was the Creole Jazz Band, unquote, says Mr. Williams. Quote, following the Dixieland Jazz Band, which recorded Livery Stable Blues and Tiger Ray, which swept the country. The Creole Band was colored and the Dixieland Band was white and they used to play across the street from each other and used to sit in…
I thought it was Celestine invented that. That's what they said, Celestine invented that. Clyde McCoy used it. Now King Oliver invented it.

Go ahead. The man who took it from King Oliver and added the plunger was Johnny Dunn, who was with Mamie Smith's Jazz Hounds and Lou Leslie's Plantation Review. It's a continuation all of the same quote. The first recording bands were the Dixieland Jazz Band. Go ahead. W.C. Smith... He played no jazz. I wonder who W.C. Smith is. Could that be Joseph Smith?
